lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion in the Solar System
top_level_objectives: Explain why Mars appears to reverse direction against the background stars from Earth.
Compare the geocentric epicycle explanation with the heliocentric explanation of retrograde motion.
Use relative motion to predict why outer planets farther from the Sun show smaller retrograde loops.
Interpret observations of planetary motion over time using two different viewing perspectives.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 1: What observers on Earth notice
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the retrograde motion puzzle as a repeated observational pattern in the night sky.
key_visuals: A night sky with constellations as a fixed star background
Mars marked as a bright red point with a path that advances eastward, slows, and loops westward
A simple calendar or sequence of dates showing the motion unfolding over weeks
student_actions: Observe how Mars changes position relative to the stars over time
Identify the moment when Mars appears to stop and reverse direction
State the basic pattern the lab will explain

scenes.brief_purpose: Show why retrograde motion was difficult to explain in a geocentric model and motivate the need for a better model.
key_visuals: An Earth-centered diagram with Mars moving on a circular path plus a small epicycle loop
A comparison label indicating 'apparent motion' versus 'real motion'
Ancient-style sky chart imagery paired with a clean explanatory overlay
student_actions: Examine how the geocentric model tries to reproduce the loop
Notice that the explanation becomes complicated and less intuitive
Reflect on why astronomers needed a more natural explanation

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3: Outside the solar system view
scenes.brief_purpose: Reframe the same event from a heliocentric perspective so students can see the true motions of Earth and Mars.
key_visuals: A solar system view with the Sun at center and Earth on a smaller, faster orbit and Mars on a larger, slower orbit
Smooth orbital paths with a highlighted segment where Earth catches up to Mars
A transparent line of sight from Earth to Mars projecting against the star background
student_actions: Watch Earth and Mars move along their orbits over time
Track the line of sight from Earth to Mars as the planets move
Connect the changing line of sight to the changing apparent position in the sky

scenes.brief_purpose: Explain the key mechanism: Earth overtakes Mars, producing the apparent backward motion.
key_visuals: An emphasized moment of Earth passing Mars on the inside track
A projected sky path showing Mars reversing direction briefly
A visual analogy with a faster car passing a slower car in an adjacent lane
student_actions: Compare the orbital speeds of Earth and Mars
Relate the overtaking event to the apparent westward loop
Use the car analogy to describe the same relative-motion effect in everyday terms

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5: Why Jupiter and Saturn loop less
scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the idea to other outer planets and show how distance from the Sun affects the size of the retrograde loop.
key_visuals: A side-by-side comparison of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn orbits
Smaller apparent loops for Jupiter and Saturn projected against the star field
A subtle speed comparison showing Earth still overtaking each planet
student_actions: Compare the magnitude of retrograde motion among the outer planets
Explain why farther planets produce less dramatic loops
Predict which planet should show the smallest apparent reversal

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate the concept that retrograde motion is an apparent effect caused by relative motion, not a true reversal of planetary motion.
key_visuals: A summary panel linking Earth-surface observations to the heliocentric orbital view
A concise before-and-after contrast between 'what we see' and 'what is happening'
A clean conceptual diagram highlighting perspective and relative motion
student_actions: Summarize the cause of retrograde motion in one or two sentences
Distinguish apparent motion from actual orbital motion
State how the heliocentric model explains the observation more naturally
